# 1. ARABIC TYPOGRAPHY

## 1.1 The strategic question first

The brief asks whether شبم should be **Kufi, modern Naskh, or custom geometric Kufi**. The answer falls out of the physics in §3 and the measurements below, and it is unambiguous:

> **Custom geometric Kufi, drawn on a flat baseline, with the three dots of ش as the brand's ownable mark.**

Three reasons, each evidenced rather than asserted:

1. **The word is structurally perfect for a flat Kufi.** شبم shapes to three base glyphs — sheen initial, beh medial, meem final — with **no ascender at all**. [MEASURED] Across the 25 faces the alif-height letters never appear; the tallest ink in the word is the sheen's shoulder. In Reem Kufi the whole word sits between the baseline and 758/1000 em, and the ب is a long horizontal bar. The word *already looks like an ice shelf* before a designer touches it. Naskh throws that away by curving the baseline.

2. **The three dots of ش are a free logo.** No competitor in MENA cold beverages owns a three-dot mark. They can become three facets, three crystals, three cubes, a triangular perforation in a cup lid, or a punch-through in the facade. [MEASURED] Dot geometry varies sharply between faces and sets the register: **Readex Pro renders them as diamonds at every weight; Changa turns them into rhombs above wght 700; Cairo turns them into hard squares at wght 900; Kufam, Alexandria, Reem Kufi and Noto Kufi keep them circular.** For an ice brand the faceted dot is the correct read, and it is a real, visible difference — see `crystal2.png`.

3. **Naskh is disqualified for the wordmark and mandatory for the verse.** [MEASURED] Amiri's tooth height is 188/1000 against an alif of 695 — a ratio of 3.70. That extreme contrast is exactly what makes Naskh beautiful for the Kaʿb b. Zuhayr line the poetry dossier recommends, and exactly what makes it illegible as a 40 mm cup logo. **Use both, in strictly separated roles.**

## 1.3 Verified licence facts — this is the section that saves money

[PRIMARY] Every family listed is **SIL Open Font License 1.1**. **Licence cost: $0.** Not "free for personal use" — genuinely free for commercial use, embedding, modification and resale of modified copies. Read verbatim from `ofl/cairo/OFL.txt`:

> "Permission is hereby granted, free of charge, to any person obtaining a copy of the Font Software, to use, study, copy, merge, embed, modify, redistribute, and sell modified and unmodified copies of the Font Software…"

The four conditions that matter commercially: the font may not be **sold by itself** (§1); the copyright notice and licence must travel with any redistributed *font file* (§2); **no Modified Version may use a Reserved Font Name** (§3); and the licence requirement **does not apply to documents created with the font** (§5) — so your packaging, menus and deck carry no obligation at all.

**Reserved Font Names, checked file by file** [PRIMARY] — this decides whether you may legally draw a custom wordmark from the face and ship the modified file:

| Family | Reserved Font Name | Can you modify and rename a derivative? |

| **Cairo** | **none** | **Yes, freely** |
| **Changa** | **none** | **Yes, freely** |

**The practical consequence, and it is worth real money:** SHABIM can take **Cairo, Changa or Kufam**, have a type designer redraw the six letters of the wordmark and the tashkīl, ship the modified file as `SHABIM Display`, and owe nobody anything. That converts what agencies normally quote as a $15,000–40,000 custom-type line into a $3,000–8,000 refinement job. **This is the single most actionable finding in this document.**

## 1.5 The two production failures I found by testing

**(a) Reem Kufi mishandles tashkīl — and this brand mandates tashkīl.** [MEASURED] The project's own README rules that the word must never travel unvocalised, because bare شبم collides with the modern medical term for phimosis. I rendered the vocalised product names in four candidate faces (`names.png`). Cairo, Changa and Kufam place shadda-over-damma on **بَلُّور** and the shadda on **القَرّ** cleanly. **Reem Kufi detaches the shadda+damma stack and floats it, and loses the shadda on القَرّ almost entirely.** Reem Kufi is therefore viable as a *display/wordmark* face where marks are drawn by hand, and **disqualified as the text face**.

**(b) The "−80" SKU name is one CSV export away from reading "80−".** [MEASURED] `financials/assumptions.json` stores the hero product as `"صَقيع ٨٠−"` — minus typed *after* the digits in logical order. Rendered (`minus.png`), the bidi algorithm reorders it and it *looks* correct. But that is luck, not design:

| String as stored | Renders as | Correct? |
|---|---|---|
| `صَقيع ٨٠−` (minus after, current) | صَقيع −٨٠ | Correct **by bidi accident** |
| `صَقيع −٨٠` (minus before) | صَقيع ٨٠− | **WRONG — reads "80 minus"** |
| `صَقيع ‎−80‎` (LRM-isolated ASCII) | صَقيع −80 | **Correct and portable** |
| superscript minus U+207B | **tofu** | Missing glyph in Cairo |

**Fix:** wrap the numeric run in U+2066 LRI … U+2069 PDI, or use the LRM-isolated ASCII form. Specify it once in the guidelines and it never breaks in a delivery-app menu field, a POS display or a spreadsheet.

## 1.7 Recommendation

**Wordmark:** commission a **custom geometric Kufi** for شَبِم, drawn from **Cairo** or **Changa** as the structural base (both have **no Reserved Font Name**, so the derivative is unencumbered). Brief the designer on three things: hold the ب as a single unbroken horizontal at the baseline; cut every terminal at 90° or 45°, never round; and **draw the three ش dots as faceted rhombs, not circles** — they are the mark.

**Display / signage:** **Cairo**, wght 200–1000. [MEASURED] The widest weight range in the entire free Arabic set, which the seasonal system in §3 needs — a 200-weight hairline for the summer "frost" register and a 900-weight for facade and signage, from one family, with the dots hardening into squares as weight rises.

**Text / UI / menus:** **Changa** (wght 200–800) or **Cairo**. Both handle tashkīl correctly, which this brand requires.

**Classical verse only:** **Amiri** (Khaled Hosny), for the Kaʿb b. Zuhayr line from *Bānat Suʿād*. Never for anything else.

**On the deck's current stack** (`deck/style.css` uses Readex Pro + IBM Plex Sans Arabic + Amiri): Readex Pro's diamond dots are genuinely on-brand and its Arabic is by Nadine Chahine, so it is a defensible choice — but see §2.3, where it measures worst of all candidates for pairing with any third-party Latin. Amiri for verse is exactly right and should stay.

# 2. BILINGUAL PAIRING — THREE PAIRINGS, MEASURED NOT ASSERTED

## 2.1 The method

"Matched x-height" is not a thing you can eyeball across scripts, because Arabic has no x-height. The two defensible anchors are:

- **T = Latin x-height ÷ Arabic tooth height** (the beh-medial bar — Arabic's optical mid-zone)
- **C = Latin cap height ÷ Arabic alif height** (the two scripts' tall zones)

**A pair works when T and C are both near 1.0 and — critically — near *each other*.** If T and C diverge, no single size setting can satisfy both, and the pair will look wrong at either display or text size. I call the gap **spread**, and it is the number that actually predicts whether a pairing survives contact with a real menu.

[MEASURED] Latin faces measured from the binaries (per 1000 em): Inter x-height **546** / cap 728 · Manrope 540/720 · Sora 534/730 · Epilogue 531/738 · Archivo 526/686 · DM Sans 526/700 · Instrument Serif 510/720 · Marcellus 500/700 · Work Sans 500/660 · Space Grotesk 486/700 · Fraunces 482/700 · Bodoni Moda 460/750 · **Jost 460/700** · Outfit 460/676 · Newsreader 426/670.

## 2.2 The three pairings

### Pairing 1 — **Cairo + Space Grotesk** · spread **0.004** · set Arabic at **97%** of Latin
**T = 0.97, C = 0.98.** [MEASURED] The best metric agreement of any pair I tested — the two scripts agree on scaling to within four thousandths. Visually verified in `pairs.png`: at 97% the Arabic and Latin sit at identical optical weight and height on a shared baseline.

**Why it works beyond the numbers.** Space Grotesk is a geometric grotesque with deliberately cut, slightly odd terminals; Cairo is a modern Kufi-sans with a flat baseline and hard joins. Both refuse to be warm. Space Grotesk's squared-off counters echo Cairo's square dots at heavy weight. Cairo's 200–1000 axis gives the system a hairline and a slab from one file, and Space Grotesk covers 300–700.

**This is my recommendation for SHABIM.** It is the pairing that best matches the ice register, and it is the only one where the metric agreement is tight enough that a franchisee's local designer cannot get the size relationship wrong.

### Pairing 2 — **Changa + Inter** · spread **0.006** · set Arabic at **116%** of Latin
**T = 1.16, C = 1.16.** [MEASURED] Perfect internal agreement, at a ratio that deliberately makes **Arabic the dominant script** — appropriate for a brand whose entire proposition is a classical Arabic word. Inter's very large x-height (546, the largest measured) is what forces the 116%.

**Why it works.** Inter is the most neutral, most screen-legible Latin available and carries no stylistic opinion — it lets Changa lead. Changa's rhomb dots above wght 700 are the crystalline read. Use this for **delivery-app menus, POS, the website and any small-size interface**, where Inter's screen performance and Changa's clarity matter more than character.

### Pairing 3 — **Kufam + Jost** · spread **0.008** · set Arabic at **92%** of Latin
**T = 0.91, C = 0.92.** [MEASURED] Excellent agreement. Kufam is by **Wael Morcos**, wght 400–900, and is the most confident, luxury-register Arabic in the free set.

**Why it works, and its one flaw.** Jost is a Futura-descendant geometric — circular bowls, single-storey a, high geometric purity — which mirrors Kufam's compass-drawn construction. Visually verified in `pairs.png`: the pairing is elegant, but **Jost's small x-height (460) makes the Latin look slightly under-scaled** next to the Arabic even at the correct ratio. Reserve this for **packaging, gift boxes and the جَنى sorbet line**, where display sizes and generous space suit it, rather than for dense menus.

| **Cairo** | **0.004** (Space Grotesk) | pairs with almost anything |

**The Readex Pro and IBM Plex Sans Arabic result needs an honest caveat, because it looks worse than it is.** Their spread is high because both have a small tooth (331 and 329) under a tall alif (740 each) — matching the tooth to a Latin x-height demands ~1.5×, matching alif to cap demands ~0.95×. **But both ship their own Latin, drawn by the same teams to be optically matched.** That is the entire point of a superfamily. So: *if you use Plex Arabic with Plex Sans, or Readex Arabic with Readex Latin, the problem does not exist.* The measurement is a warning against **mixing them with a third-party Latin**, which is exactly what a franchisee's local designer will eventually do.

**Demonstrated in `pairs.png`:** Reem Kufi + Space Grotesk at a naive 100% leaves the Arabic visibly smaller and lighter than the Latin; corrected to the tooth-matched 131%, the Arabic balances but the tall alif of الماء now overshoots the Latin cap line. You can satisfy one anchor or the other, never both. That is what spread 0.44 looks like in practice.

# 3. COLOUR — COMPUTED FROM PUBLISHED OPTICAL CONSTANTS

## 3.1 Why thick ice is blue — the actual physics, with the actual numbers

The usual explanation ("water absorbs red") is true but useless to a designer because it carries no magnitude. Here is the real mechanism with measured values.

**Source data [PRIMARY]:** S. G. Warren and R. E. Brandt, *"Optical constants of ice from the ultraviolet to the microwave: A revised compilation,"* **J. Geophys. Res. 113, D14220 (2008)**, doi:10.1029/2007JD009744. Ice at **−7 °C**, 486 tabulated wavelengths. Retrieved from the CC0 refractiveindex.info database (Polyanskiy, *Scientific Data* **11**, 94, 2024, doi:10.1038/s41597-023-02898-2).

**The mechanism.** Ice is transparent because it has no electronic absorption in the visible — the O–H bond's electronic transitions sit deep in the UV. What little absorption exists in the visible is the **high-order vibrational overtone series of the O–H stretch**. [MEASURED] I located the fundamental directly in the Warren & Brandt table: the strongest absorption peak in the near-IR is at **3077 nm = 3250 cm⁻¹**, with k = 0.625 and α = 2.55 × 10⁶ m⁻¹. Its harmonics fall at:

| harmonic | wavelength | where it lands |
|---|---|---|
| n = 2 | 1550 nm | near-IR (measured local max at 1493 nm) |
| n = 3 | 1033 nm | near-IR |
| n = 4 | 775 nm | far red |
| **n = 5** | **620 nm** | **orange-red — visible** |
| **n = 6** | **517 nm** | **green — visible, very weak** |

**So the blue of ice is the fifth and sixth harmonic of a molecular vibration.** That is the sentence for the deck. Anharmonicity makes each successive overtone roughly an order of magnitude weaker, which is precisely why the effect needs metres of path length to become visible.

**The magnitudes** [MEASURED], α = 4πk/λ:

| λ | k | α (m⁻¹) | penetration depth 1/α |
|---|---|---|---|
| 400 nm | 2.365 × 10⁻¹¹ | 0.00066 | **1,346 m** |
| 450 nm | 9.239 × 10⁻¹¹ | 0.0026 | **388 m** |
| 500 nm | 5.889 × 10⁻¹⁰ | 0.0148 | 68 m |
| 550 nm | 2.289 × 10⁻⁹ | 0.0523 | 19 m |
| 600 nm | 5.730 × 10⁻⁹ | 0.120 | 8.3 m |
| 650 nm | 1.430 × 10⁻⁸ | 0.277 | 3.6 m |
| **700 nm** | 2.900 × 10⁻⁸ | **0.521** | **1.92 m** |
| 750 nm | 5.870 × 10⁻⁸ | 0.984 | 1.02 m |

**The headline numbers:**
- **α(700 nm) / α(450 nm) = 202×.** Ice absorbs red light two hundred times more strongly than blue.
- **Absorption minimum at 390 nm, α = 0.00064 m⁻¹ — a penetration depth of 1,552 m.** Violet light travels a mile and a half through pure ice. Red light gets 1.9 metres.
- That ratio is what makes ice blue. Nothing is added; red is subtracted.

**Two mechanisms, and the brand needs both.** Snow and bubbly ice are *white* because multiple scattering off air inclusions returns light before it accumulates path length. Clear ice is *blue* because scattering has been removed and absorption accumulates. **The SHABIM ice block is a scattering-free object by manufacturing intent — directional freezing exists precisely to eliminate bubbles — which means it is optically a piece of glacier, at glacier physics, at 12 cm instead of 12 m.**

This is the most commercially important line in this section. The القالَب / بَلُّور vessel **will not photograph blue by itself**. Every blue in the customer's photograph has to be engineered:

1. **Edge lighting.** Ice has n ≈ 1.309 at 550 nm [MEASURED, Warren & Brandt]. Critical angle = arcsin(1/1.309) = **49.9°**. Light injected into a cut face totally-internally-reflects and travels the block's *long* path, so a 12 cm block edge-lit along its length behaves optically like a much longer path. **Blue LEDs at the base of the serving tray, aimed into a polished facet, are not decoration — they are the mechanism that makes the product look like what it is.**
2. **Background, not material.** A `#00BFFF` under-tray or backlit panel reads through the block as the block's own colour.
3. **Cut geometry.** Facets create caustics and refracted highlights; a smooth cylinder creates none. **Specify facets.**
4. **Do not tint the ice.** A blue-dyed block reads as syrup and destroys the "pure water, carved" story that justifies a 15,000 IQD price.

## 4.2 The three changes I recommend

### (a) القالَب → **بَلُّور** · *ballūr* · "crystal"

**القالَب** means "the mould" — the thing you cast *in*, not the thing you serve. It names the tooling, not the product. It is also flat: nothing about it says cold, clear, or precious.

**بَلُّور** (also بِلَّوْر) is classical Arabic for **rock crystal / clear crystal**, long established in the lexica and in classical poetry as the standard simile for anything transparent and precious. It is the exact word an Arab poet reaches for when describing clear ice.

**Why it works commercially:** it is the only name in the range that describes the *material state* the whole product exists to demonstrate. At 15,000 IQD (US $9.80) this is the highest-priced item on the menu and it must justify itself in one word. "Crystal" does. "Mould" does not. [MEASURED] It also renders cleanly with its shadda+damma stack in Cairo, Changa and Kufam (`names.png`).

**Vocalise as بَلُّور.** Romanise as **Ballour** for menus (not *Ballūr* — macrons do not survive a POS system) and *ballūr* in the guidelines.

### (b) رَذاذ → split into **رَذاذ** (juice) and **بَرَد** (slush)

**رَذاذ** (*radhādh*, fine drizzle / spray) is lovely for **fresh-pressed juice** — it carries lightness and freshness.

But the slush is a different object, and Arabic has the exact word: **بَرَد** (*barad*) — **hail**. Frozen pellets of water falling from the sky. That is, physically and precisely, what a slush is.

**The resonance is the point:** the master brand line is «شَبِم · بَرْدُ الماء» (*bardu-l-mā'*, with sukūn). The slush is **بَرَد** (*barad*, with fatḥa). Same root, one diacritic apart, two different words. **This is exactly the discipline the README already mandates** — the brand must always vocalise anyway because of the شَبَم/شَبِم medical collision. بَرَد turns that constraint into a feature: the tashkīl is doing semantic work, visibly, on the menu.

⚠️ **One caution:** بَرَد appears in the Qur'an in the context of hail. **A single common noun is not Qur'anic text** and carries no restriction — the poetry dossier's prohibition is on *printing Qur'anic verses* on disposable packaging, which this is not. But have an Iraqi religious-affairs advisor confirm before print. Cost of asking: one phone call.

### (c) لَفائِف — keep, but know the risk

**لَفائِف** is correct for rolled ice cream. **The collision:** in Iraqi and Levantine food contexts لفائف overwhelmingly means **savoury wraps** — shawarma, saj rolls. A hungry Baghdadi reading لَفائِف on a menu may expect chicken.

**Options:** (1) keep it and always lock it to an image, which the format demands anyway since the product is made live; (2) switch to **رَقائِق** (*raqā'iq*, "thin sheets/wafers"), which is more literally accurate — the product *is* a thin frozen sheet scraped off a pan — and carries no savoury association.

**My recommendation: keep لَفائِف, add the image lock as a guideline rule.** The word is warmer and the theatre of the pan resolves the ambiguity in three seconds. **But test it** — this is exactly the kind of thing open question #8 in the README is for.

## 5.1 The closest strategic reference, and why

**It is Aesop — with %Arabica as the mark strategy and Kaak Al Manara as the cultural thesis.** Not the obvious answer, so here is the argument.

The obvious pick is %Arabica, because it is a beverage brand with a great glyph. But %Arabica solves a *retail* problem SHABIM does not have. SHABIM's hardest identity problem is this: **the brand's core asset is a physical, transparent, melting object that will be built by different contractors in Baghdad, Riyadh, Dubai and Amman at wildly different budgets** — a $448,784 prototype Cube and a $168,792 franchised Shard, per the model. A conventional identity system, which replicates a template, **will fail at the third franchisee** when the ice-cube facade is value-engineered into blue plastic.

**Aesop is the only brand on this list that solved exactly that.** Every Aesop store is different — different architect, different material, different budget — and every one is unmistakably Aesop, because the identity is codified as **material rules and typographic discipline** rather than as a replicated look. That is the only kind of system that survives franchising a *building* rather than a *logo*.

**So the strategic reference is:**
- **Aesop** for how the system is *written* — material rules, one typeface, restraint, no template.
- **%Arabica** for the *mark* — the three ش dots as a script-free, scale-free glyph that carries the brand with no word attached.
- **Kaak Al Manara** for the *story* — SHABIM is not importing a novelty; Baghdad already buys a block of ice every summer day at **IQD 4,000** [SESSION-VERIFIED, Al-Araby Al-Jadeed / 964media]. SHABIM makes the ice the product instead of the packaging.
